claims.text: Structural and chemical stability is governed by the balance between configurational-entropy stabilization and temperature-driven atomic diffusion.
Temperature-driven atomic diffusion promotes local chemical ordering or segregation.
Nanoparticles with more favorable local atomic interactions will resist phase separation and compositional segregation at high temperatures.
The initial nanoparticles are near-equiatomic, contain at least five metals, and are single-phase solid solutions with randomly mixed atoms.
Prolonged exposure at each temperature step permits sufficient atomic diffusion.
Differential inter-element bonding energies induce local chemical short-range order.
Atomic diffusion is enhanced at operational temperatures.
In nanoparticles dominated by favorable local interactions, configurational entropy offsets the tendency toward phase separation.
Differences in bonding energies can cause atomic segregation and diffusion-driven phase separation.
Diffusion-driven phase separation undermines structural and chemical stability.
Nanoparticles engineered to have enhanced favorable local ordering will retain a single-phase solid-solution structure with minimal segregation over 473–1923 K.
Nanoparticles lacking favorable local ordering will exhibit compositional segregation, secondary phases, or morphological degradation.
The proposed mechanism applies only when particle-size and surface effects do not dominate bulk diffusion effects.
Oxidizing or restructuring atmospheres can introduce stability changes unrelated to inherent alloy stability.
The relevant temperature thresholds and the relative contributions of configurational entropy and bonding enthalpy vary with elemental combination.
Surface energy and particle-support interactions can modulate the predicted stability behavior.
Controlled annealing or modified synthesis protocols can produce nanoparticles with greater local chemical ordering than a randomized control.
